h1: Can an SEO agency guarantee rankings? No. Here's what can be guaranteed.
metaDescription: No agency can guarantee a Google ranking position. A guarantee against your own frozen baseline can be written and enforced — here's exactly how to do it.
answer: No honest SEO agency guarantees a ranking position, because nobody controls Google's index and Google's own guidance tells you to be wary of anyone who promises a number one spot. What can be guaranteed is movement against a metric you both freeze in writing on day one — usually qualified organic leads over a trailing 90 days.
takeaways: A position guarantee is unenforceable by design. The party promising it doesn't control the system delivering it.
Most "guarantees" that survive contact with a lawyer are engineered to be technically true — the keyword set is chosen after you sign.
A **baseline guarantee** is different: it names a number that already exists in your business, freezes it, and attaches a remedy.
The remedy matters more than the promise. A refund gives you your money back and no rankings; continued free work at least keeps compounding.

sections.h2: Why a position guarantee can't be honoured
body: Not "shouldn't". Can't. The agency promising it has no mechanism to deliver it, and there is no support channel, escalation path or account manager at Google who can move a page up a results page. The index isn't for sale, and the ranking systems aren't reachable from outside.
Even if you set aside the control problem, the thing being promised doesn't have a single value. There is no one search results page any more.
bullets: **Results vary by location, device, language and history.** "Position 3" in Bangalore on mobile can be position 8 in Delhi on desktop, for the same query on the same day.
**The page layout keeps changing.** An AI Overview, a map pack or four ad slots above you means position 1 organic is now well below the fold, and the click-through you were sold never arrives.
**Competitors act.** Yours can hire someone better next quarter. Nobody can guarantee an outcome that depends on other people's decisions.
**Core updates reshuffle whole categories** several times a year, and Google publishes no per-site diagnosis you can appeal against.
**Rank trackers disagree with each other**, so even verifying the promise is contestable — which is convenient for whoever made it.

sections.h2: What Google itself says about it
body: You don't have to take an agency's word for this. Google's own guidance on hiring an SEO explicitly warns businesses about anyone who guarantees a number one ranking, and lists it among the signals of a service worth avoiding. That documentation has said essentially the same thing for well over a decade.

It's worth reading before you take a sales call, because it reframes the conversation. A ranking guarantee isn't a bold commitment from a confident agency. It's a claim the platform itself has flagged, made by someone who either doesn't know that or is counting on you not knowing it.

callout.title: The uncomfortable follow-up
callout.body: There is one way to move a competitive keyword fast and reliably: buy links. It works, right up until it doesn't, and the recovery costs more than the retainer ever saved. When a guarantee comes with a suspiciously short timeline, this is usually the mechanism underneath it.

sections.h2: Five guarantees engineered to be technically true
body: Most ranking guarantees aren't outright lies. They're carefully constructed to be kept without anything useful happening. Knowing the construction is how you spot it in a proposal.

sections.h2: What a baseline guarantee measures instead
body: The honest alternative doesn't promise a position on Google. It promises movement in a number that already exists inside your business, measured against where that number stood before anyone touched anything.

Ours is specific: the trailing 90 days of qualified leads from organic search, counted in your CRM, frozen in writing on day one. If we haven't beaten it within 90 days, we keep working at no charge until we do. That's not generosity — it's why we cap ourselves at three new clients a month. You cannot carry that exposure across thirty accounts and still mean it.

The reason this version is enforceable and a ranking promise isn't comes down to one thing: the number is ours to influence and yours to verify. Nobody has to interpret a rank tracker. You open your CRM.

callout.title: Why leads and not traffic
callout.body: Traffic is inflatable. Rank a page for a broad informational query and you can double sessions without a single extra enquiry. Leads resist that, which is exactly why fewer agencies will sign up to them.

sections.h2: How to write a baseline into the contract
body: A guarantee that isn't specified precisely turns into a negotiation at exactly the moment you have least leverage. Eight clauses is usually enough, and any competent agency can complete them in one meeting.
numbered: **The metric, named exactly.** Not "leads" — "form submissions and inbound calls from non-brand organic sessions, marked qualified by the sales team".
**The source of truth.** One system wins when two disagree. Usually the CRM, because that's what pays salaries.
**The freeze.** The trailing 90 days ending the day before work starts, written into the contract as an actual number, not a formula to be calculated later.
**The definition of qualified**, plus who decides in a borderline case and how a dispute is resolved.
**The exclusions.** Branded search, paid traffic, existing customers, spam submissions. State them, or you'll argue about them.
**The measurement window and read date.** A fixed calendar date, so nobody renegotiates the deadline in month three.
**The remedy.** What actually happens if the number isn't beaten — in the same paragraph, not a separate annexure.
**Your obligations.** A deployment SLA for fixes and an approval SLA for content. A guarantee with no client-side duty is either priced defensively or not meant seriously.

body: Seasonality. If your baseline quarter was Diwali and your measurement quarter is January, you've handed the agency an unwinnable target — or, reversed, an unearned win. Either compare like-for-like against the same quarter last year, or agree an adjustment in advance. More on this in [how to set an SEO baseline](/journal/how-to-set-an-seo-baseline).

sections.h2: Refunds, free work and getting out
body: The remedy is the guarantee. Everything before it is framing. There are three shapes it takes, and the one that sounds best is usually the weakest.

**A refund** returns your money and leaves you where you started, minus a quarter. It's the easiest to sell and the least useful, because the cost of a failed engagement was never mainly the fee — it was the three months your competitors spent publishing.

**Continued free work** keeps the compounding alive and puts the agency's costs on the line rather than just their margin. It's the version that actually hurts to honour, which is why so few offer it. It's ours.

**A clean exit** is the floor, and it should exist regardless of the remedy: month-to-month after the first quarter, 30 days' notice, and you keep every asset — content, accounts, data, link placements, all of it. An agency that holds your Search Console hostage on the way out was never aligned with you.

If you're comparing proposals, [what should be in an SEO contract](/answers/what-should-be-in-an-seo-contract) covers the rest of the paperwork, and [our pricing](/pricing) shows what we charge to carry this risk.

faqs.a: Guaranteed rankings usually are, or are engineered to be meaningless. Guaranteed work isn't the same thing as guaranteed results, and a guarantee tied to a metric inside your own business — leads, revenue — can be entirely legitimate. The test is whether the number was frozen before work started and whether a remedy is written down.

faqs.q: Why can't anyone guarantee a #1 ranking on Google?
faqs.a: Because the agency doesn't control the index and can't influence competitors, core updates or the layout of the results page. Google's own guidance on hiring an SEO warns against anyone promising a number one position. There's also no verification standard — two rank trackers will report different positions for the same query.

faqs.q: What can an SEO agency actually guarantee?
faqs.a: Scope, cadence and process, always. Beyond that, an outcome guarantee is possible if it's tied to a metric you both freeze at the start — qualified organic leads, organic revenue, or non-brand converting sessions. Ours is movement against your trailing 90-day organic lead count, with free continued work if we miss it.

faqs.q: Should I avoid agencies that offer guarantees?
faqs.a: Avoid position guarantees. Don't avoid outcome guarantees, since an agency willing to attach a consequence to its work is rarer and usually more disciplined about scope. Read which kind you're being offered: if the promise names a Google position, walk. If it names a number from your own accounts, keep reading.

faqs.q: What if my SEO agency guaranteed rankings and failed?
faqs.a: Check the conditions clause before anything else — most such guarantees are voided by ordinary client behaviour like editing a draft or approving late. If the guarantee is genuinely unmet and the contract states a remedy, pursue it in writing. If no remedy was stated, the promise was marketing, and the practical response is to leave cleanly with your assets.
